objective: Apply bundling adjustment and the termination limit together
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: Six current-carrying 10 AWG THHN copper conductors are installed in one EMT run longer than 24 in. Ambient is 30°C and all terminations are rated 75°C. What is the conductors' allowable ampacity?
math: Start at the 90°C column (THHN): 10 AWG Cu = 40 A
Termination check (75°C column): 10 AWG Cu = 35 A
Allowable ampacity = the lower of 32 A and 35 A = 32 A
center: Derate from the insulation's own temperature column (90°C for THHN), then check that the result does not exceed the termination column (75°C). Here 32 A is below 35 A, so 32 A stands.
28 A is the trap: it applies the 80% to the 75°C value. 40 A forgets the adjustment. 35 A forgets the adjustment but applies the termination limit.
more: This answer is the conductor's ampacity, not its breaker size. 240.4(D)(7) still caps 10 AWG copper at 30 A — see the next question.
navTip: Tab Table 310.16 and the adjustment table, Table 310.15(C)(1), so you can flip between them quickly.

objective: Apply the small-conductor rule after derating
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: The 10 AWG copper conductors in the previous question have an adjusted ampacity of 32 A. What is the largest standard overcurrent device permitted to protect them (no special exceptions apply)?
center: 240.4(D) overrides the 'next size up' rule for 14, 12 and 10 AWG. Even though 32 A would normally round up to 35 A, 10 AWG copper is capped at 30 A.
navTip: 240.4(D) sits right after the 'next size up' rule in 240.4(B) — read them as a pair.

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: Three current-carrying 6 AWG THWN-2 copper conductors run in conduit where the ambient temperature is 40°C (104°F). Using the 90°C column, what is the corrected ampacity?
center: Three conductors means no bundling adjustment (that starts at four). Only the ambient correction applies.
57 A uses the 75°C column and its 0.88 factor; 65 A is the uncorrected 75°C value; 75 A ignores the heat.
more: With 75°C terminations the circuit would still be limited to 65 A (110.14(C)), because 68 A is above the 75°C column value.
ref: Table 310.16; ambient correction table — NEC 2020 Table 310.15(B)(1); NEC 2023 Table 310.15(B)(1)(1).
navTip: In the 2023 book the 30°C-based correction table is labeled 310.15(B)(1)(1); a second table based on 40°C follows it. Use the one that matches the ampacity table you are reading.
status: Verified (2023 table label: confirm on your page)

objective: Size feeder overcurrent protection for mixed loads
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A feeder supplies 100 A of continuous load and 40 A of noncontinuous load. What is the minimum standard rating of the feeder overcurrent device?
center: Only the continuous part gets the 125%. 140 A forgets the factor entirely; 150 A is below the 165 A minimum.
navTip: Feeders are Article 215 — the 125% continuous rule is in 215.2 (conductors) and 215.3 (overcurrent device).

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A feeder is protected by a 200-A circuit breaker. What is the minimum size copper equipment grounding conductor?
center: Table 250.122 is read by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of the conductor: 200 A → 6 AWG copper (4 AWG aluminum).
more: If the ungrounded conductors were upsized for voltage drop, 250.122(B) would require the EGC to be increased proportionally.
navTip: Two grounding tables trip people: 250.122 = EGC (by breaker size); 250.66 = GEC (by service conductor size). Tab them in different colors.

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A service uses 3/0 AWG copper service-entrance conductors. What is the minimum size copper grounding electrode conductor to a metal underground water pipe electrode?
center: Table 250.66: 2/0 or 3/0 copper service conductors → 4 AWG copper GEC.
6 AWG is the cap only for the portion going to rod, pipe, or plate electrodes (250.66(A)). A water pipe electrode doesn't get that reduction.
navTip: Read Table 250.66 by the largest ungrounded service conductor (or equivalent area for parallel sets).

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A service has a single set of 500 kcmil copper ungrounded conductors. What is the minimum size copper main bonding jumper?
center: 250.28(D) sends you to Table 250.102(C)(1). Over 350 through 600 kcmil copper → 1/0 AWG copper.
Above 1100 kcmil copper, the jumper must be at least 12.5% of the area of the largest ungrounded conductor instead of using the table rows.
navTip: Main bonding jumper, system bonding jumper, supply-side bonding jumper and the minimum service neutral all use Table 250.102(C)(1).

objective: Apply the dwelling general lighting load and demand factors
stem: A 2,000 sq ft dwelling has the general lighting load plus the two required small-appliance circuits and one laundry circuit. After applying the lighting demand factors, what is the demand load for these items?
math: General lighting: 2,000 sq ft × 3 VA = 6,000 VA
center: Small-appliance and laundry loads are added to the lighting load BEFORE the demand factors are applied (220.52).
3,675 VA applies 35% to everything; 10,500 VA skips the demand step; 6,000 VA counts only the lighting.
more: Edition map: 2020 puts the 3 VA/sq ft in Table 220.12 and the demand factors in Table 220.42. The 2023 NEC moved them to 220.41 and Table 220.45. Same numbers, different pages — tab whichever book you bring.
navTip: In a 2023 book, dwelling feeder/service calcs start at Part III (220.40). Don't hunt for the 3 VA in Table 220.12 — in 2023 that table is non-dwelling only (now 220.42).

objective: Apply Table 220.55 Note 1 for a range over 12 kW
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: What is the demand load for one 14-kW household range, using Table 220.55 Column C and its notes?
math: Column C, 1 appliance = 8 kW (for ranges up to 12 kW)
center: Column C assumes ranges of 12 kW or less. Note 1 bumps the Column C value 5% for each kW (or major fraction) over 12 kW.
navTip: The table notes are where the real rules live. Highlight Note 1 the same color as Column C.

objective: Recall the optional dwelling calculation percentages
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: Under the optional dwelling calculation in 220.82(B), the first 10 kVA of 'general load' is taken at 100%. The remainder is taken at:
center: 220.82(B): first 10 kVA at 100%, remainder at 40%. Heating and air-conditioning are added separately under 220.82(C).
35% is the standard-method lighting demand factor — a different table.
navTip: Optional method is Part IV of Article 220 (220.82). Tab it separately from the standard method.

objective: Size one-family dwelling service conductors with the 83% rule
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A 200-A service supplies the entire load of a one-family dwelling. Using the 83% rule of 310.12 and the 75°C column, what is the minimum copper service conductor?
center: 310.12 lets 100–400 A one-family dwelling service conductors carry only 83% of the service rating. 3/0 AWG is what you'd get at 100% (200 A in the 75°C column).
navTip: 310.12 applies only to dwelling services and main feeders that carry the entire load. Don't use it for subpanels that serve part of the load.

objective: Size motor branch-circuit conductors from the table FLC
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A 25-hp, 460-V, three-phase squirrel-cage motor (continuous duty) has a nameplate FLA of 32 A. What is the minimum copper branch-circuit conductor, using the 75°C column?
math: Table 430.250: 25 hp, 460 V = 34 A (use the table, not the nameplate)
Table 310.16, 75°C Cu: 10 AWG = 35 A (too small), 8 AWG = 50 A
center: Conductor sizing uses the table FLC (430.6(A)(1)). The 32 A nameplate value is a distractor for this step.
navTip: Motor tables are at the back of Article 430: 430.247 (DC), 430.248 (1-phase), 430.250 (3-phase).

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: For the same 25-hp, 460-V motor (table FLC 34 A), what is the maximum inverse-time circuit breaker rating permitted, using the next-higher-size allowance?
math: 85 A is not a standard size (240.6(A))
430.52(C)(1) Exception No. 1: next higher standard size = 90 A
center: 85 A is the calculated value, but it isn't a standard rating — the exception lets you go to the next standard size up, 90 A. 100 A would require Exception No. 2 (motor won't start).
navTip: Table 430.52 is organized by motor type down the side and device type across the top — find the column before the row.

objective: Size motor overload protection from the nameplate
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: The same motor's nameplate shows FLA 32 A and a service factor of 1.15. What is the maximum rating of a separate overload device under the basic rule?
math: 430.32(A)(1): service factor 1.15 or more → 125% of nameplate FLA
center: Overloads use the NAMEPLATE current. 42.5 A is 125% of the table value (wrong current). 36.8 A uses 115% (that's for motors without the 1.15 service factor or 40°C rise marking).
navTip: Three motor numbers, three places: conductors 430.22 (table), OCPD 430.52 (table), overloads 430.32 (nameplate).

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A feeder supplies two 460-V, three-phase motors with table FLCs of 34 A and 21 A, and no other loads. What is the minimum feeder conductor ampacity?
math: 430.24: 125% of the largest motor + 100% of the others
center: Only the largest motor gets the 125%. 68.8 A multiplies both motors by 125%; 55 A adds them at 100%.
navTip: 430.24 is the 'several motors' rule; 430.62 is the matching rule for the feeder's overcurrent device.

edition: Theory (Ugly's) + NEC
stem: A 75-kVA, three-phase transformer has a 480-V primary. What is the rated primary current?
center: 156.3 A forgets the 1.732 (single-phase formula). 208.2 A is the 208-V secondary current. 52.1 A divides by 1.732 twice.
ref: Ugly's — three-phase formulas; used with Table 450.3(B).
navTip: Tab the Ugly's three-phase formula page. Don't write formulas on tabs — the test center allows highlighting, underlining and permanent tabs only.

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: That 75-kVA, 480-V transformer (primary current 90.2 A) is protected on the primary only. What is the maximum standard primary overcurrent device permitted under Table 450.3(B)?
math: Primary-only protection, primary current 9 A or more → 125%
Note 1: where 125% does not match a standard size, the next higher standard size is permitted
center: 110 A rounds down. 225 A is the 250% figure used when secondary protection is also provided.
navTip: Table 450.3(A) is over 1000 V; 450.3(B) is 1000 V and less. Most exam questions are 450.3(B).

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: The conductors from a generator's output terminals to the first distribution device containing overcurrent protection must have an ampacity of not less than what percentage of the generator's nameplate current rating?
center: 445.13(A): 115% of the nameplate current rating. 125% is the continuous-load factor people reach for out of habit.
navTip: Generators are Article 445 — short article, worth one tab.

objective: Apply nameplate maximum overcurrent rating for HVAC equipment
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A rooftop air-conditioning unit's nameplate lists 'MAX FUSE/BREAKER 40 A'. The installer wants a 45-A breaker because it's in stock. This is:
choices: Permitted if the conductors are rated 45 A
Permitted if the unit is outdoors
Not permitted — the marked maximum overcurrent rating may not be exceeded
Permitted if the unit has a service disconnect
center: 440.22(C) and 110.3(B): where the equipment is marked with a maximum fuse or breaker size, the protective device may not exceed that marking.
navTip: In Article 440, sizing starts at 440.6 (RLA/BCSC); overcurrent device limits are 440.22.

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: An electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) unit has a maximum load of 48 A. What is the minimum standard overcurrent device rating for its branch circuit?
math: 625.41: OCPD sized for continuous duty, not less than 125% of the maximum EVSE load
center: EV charging is treated as continuous. 50 A would be undersized (only 104%).
navTip: EV charging = Article 625. Remember '6-2-5 = 1-2-5%'.

stem: A PV source circuit has a module short-circuit current (Isc) of 10 A. Using the 125% method, what is the circuit's maximum current?
center: 15.6 A (Isc × 1.56) is the conductor ampacity / OCPD sizing figure — that's 125% applied twice (690.8(B) adds another 125% for continuous duty).
navTip: PV is Article 690; the two 125% steps are (A) maximum current, then (B) conductor/OCPD sizing.

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: Wiring from an emergency source to emergency loads must generally be:
choices: Kept entirely independent of all other wiring and equipment, except as permitted
Run in the same raceway as normal power for redundancy
center: 700.10(B): emergency circuit wiring is kept entirely independent of all other wiring. The listed exceptions (transfer equipment enclosures, exit signs with two sources, etc.) are narrow.
navTip: Article 700 (emergency) vs 701 (legally required) vs 702 (optional): the separation rule is strict only in 700.

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A Class 2 thermostat cable is to be pulled into a raceway that contains 120-V power conductors. In general, this is:
choices: Permitted if the Class 2 cable is rated 300 V
Not permitted unless separated by a barrier or another specific allowance applies
Permitted if the raceway is metal
center: 725.136(A): Class 2 and Class 3 circuits are not placed in the same raceway, cable, or enclosure with power conductors except as specifically permitted (barriers, segregation in enclosures, etc.). Insulation rating alone doesn't make it legal.
navTip: In the 2023 NEC, Article 725 was split: general rules are in 722, Class 1 moved to 724, Class 2/3 stayed in 725.

objective: Locate a conduit seal in Class I, Division 1
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: In a Class I, Division 1 location, a conduit seal is required for a conduit entering an enclosure that contains arcing devices. The seal must be installed within what distance of the enclosure?
center: 501.15(A)(1): seals within 450 mm (18 in.) of the enclosure, and only listed fittings (unions, couplings, etc.) between the seal and the enclosure.
navTip: Article 501 = Class I wiring. .10 = wiring methods, .15 = sealing.

objective: Locate the classified area in a major repair garage
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: In a major repair garage where vehicles using gasoline are repaired (ventilation not used to reduce the area), the floor area is generally classified Class I, Division 2 up to what height above the floor?
center: Gasoline vapor is heavier than air, so the classified area is measured up from the floor: 450 mm (18 in.).
ref: 511.3(C) (major repair garages; check the exact subdivision in your edition).
navTip: Article 511 = repair garages; 514 = fuel dispensing. Both measure the 18-in. zone from the floor.
status: Verified (subdivision label: confirm on your page)

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: At a dwelling with a permanently installed pool, at least one 125-V, 15- or 20-A receptacle on a general-purpose branch circuit must be located not less than 6 ft and not more than how far from the inside wall of the pool?
center: 680.22(A)(3): not less than 1.83 m (6 ft) and not more than 6.0 m (20 ft) from the inside wall, and not more than 2.0 m (6 ft 6 in.) above the floor or grade.
navTip: 680.22 = area lighting, receptacles and equipment around pools. Highlight the three distances in (A).

objective: Calculate conduit fill with mixed conductor sizes
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: Three 6 AWG THHN and one 10 AWG THHN copper conductors will be installed in EMT. What is the smallest trade size permitted?
math: Chapter 9, Table 5 (THHN): 6 AWG = 0.0507 in², 10 AWG = 0.0211 in²
center: Mixed sizes mean you can't use Annex C — add up the conductor areas from Table 5 and compare to the 40% column for EMT in Table 4.
navTip: Table 4 is grouped by raceway type; find the EMT block first, then the 40% column.

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: A 4 in. × 1-1/2 in. square box with internal cable clamps contains one receptacle and two 12/2 NM cables with grounds (four insulated 12 AWG conductors and two bare grounds). What volume is required?
math: Total = 8 × 2.25 cu in. (12 AWG) = 18.00 cu in.
center: A 4 × 1-1/2 square box is 21.0 cu in. (Table 314.16(A)), so this fits. 20.25 counts each ground separately; 15.75 forgets the clamps; 22.50 counts each clamp separately.
navTip: 314.16(B)(1)–(5) is the counting rulebook. Tab it, and tab Table 314.16(A) for box volumes.

objective: Size a pull box for an angle pull
edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: An angle pull has two 3-in. conduits and one 2-in. conduit entering the same wall of a pull box. What is the minimum distance from that wall to the opposite wall?
math: 314.28(A)(2): 6 × largest raceway + sum of the other raceways in the same row on the same wall
center: 18 in. forgets the other raceways. 24 in. is the straight-pull rule (8 × 3 in.).
navTip: Straight pull = 8 ×; angle or U pull = 6 × + others. Both are 314.28(A).

edition: NEC 2020 or 2023 (same rule; numbering noted where it differs)
stem: Underground service conductors that are not encased in concrete and are buried 18 in. or more below grade must have a warning ribbon placed in the trench at least how far above the installation?
center: 300.5(D)(3): warning ribbon at least 300 mm (12 in.) above the underground installation.
navTip: 300.5 is the whole underground rule set: (A) cover table, (D) protection from damage, (G) sealing.

objective: Calculate single-phase voltage drop with the K formula
edition: Ugly's / NEC Chapter 9 Table 8
stem: A 120-V, 16-A load is 150 ft (one way) from the panel on 12 AWG copper (6,530 cmil). Using K = 12.9, what is the approximate voltage drop?
math: 9.5 V ÷ 120 V ≈ 7.9% — well over the 3% branch-circuit recommendation
center: 4.7 V forgets the 2 (single-phase has two conductors in the loop). For three-phase the 2 becomes 1.732.
ref: Ugly's voltage drop formula; Chapter 9, Table 8 (circular mils); 210.19(A) Informational Note (recommendation).
navTip: Chapter 9 Table 8 gives cmil for each size — tab it next to your Ugly's voltage-drop page.

edition: NFPA 70E 2024
stem: Under NFPA 70E (2024) 120.6, where must the absence of voltage be tested?
choices: At each phase conductor or circuit part at each point of work
Anywhere on the circuit, if the tester is verified first
center: The 2024 edition added 'at each point of work' — testing upstream or at the panel doesn't prove the parts you will touch are dead. The tester is verified on a known source before and after the test.
navTip: In the 2024 book the step list moved from 120.5 to 120.6. Re-tab it if your tabs came from a 2021 class.

edition: Plan reading (blueprint packet)
stem: An electrical plan is drawn at 1/8 in. = 1 ft. A feeder run measures 6-1/2 in. on the drawing. What is the actual length?
math: At 1/8 in. = 1 ft, every 1 in. on the drawing = 8 ft
center: 26 ft uses 1/4 in. = 1 ft. Read the scale printed on the sheet, not the one on the cover page — sheets can differ.
ref: Physical blueprint packet (handed out at the test center); general plan-reading practice.
navTip: On test day, check the title block of each sheet for its scale before measuring.
